title: Brigid of Kildare
hook: abbess and legend-maker; her cross is woven from rushes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patrick's Confession, a book that opens with a man calling himself a sinner. Your line was I, a sinner. What honest sentence did you write about yourself? Day seven hundred forty-seven.

A handful of green rushes, pulled from a riverbank. Fold one over another, turn, fold again, turn, and a small square grows in the middle with four arms reaching out. Tie the ends with a bit of thread. In Ireland people still make these, and hang them over the door or in the kitchen, where they stay until the next one replaces them. It's called Brigid's cross. The woman it's named for ran a great double community of nuns and monks in Ireland, and so many stories gathered around her that it's hard to see where the woman ends and the legend begins. Today, Brigid.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF RUSHES.` → `OVER THE DOOR.` → `BRIGID'S CROSS.`

segments.voice: Start with an early life of her, written by a monk of Kildare named Cogitosus. He says plainly that he's writing down what he heard from older people. So from the first page, we're in the land of memory, not records. Cogitosus tells of a woman whose hands were always open. She gave food and clothing away so often that, in his telling, what she gave kept coming back: butter that didn't run out, milk that stretched to feed more guests than it should have. One story is pure delight. Coming in from the rain, she hung her wet cloak on a beam of sunlight, mistaking it for a wooden beam, and the cloak hung there, drying, as if on a peg. Next, the work. Cogitosus describes Kildare as a large community where both women and men lived under her care, with a church where they prayed, and people coming from all over for help. An abbess is the woman who leads a community of nuns. Brigid led one so well that it became a place people traveled toward. Now the cross. The rush cross isn't in Cogitosus. It comes from a later story people tell: Brigid sitting beside a dying man who did not know Christ, picking up rushes from the floor, and weaving a cross while she told him who Jesus was. In the story, he asks to be baptized before he dies. Some tellings make the man her father, some a chieftain. Whatever happened by that bed, the cross outlived it. Rushes are about the plainest thing a person could pick up: free, damp, growing at the water's edge. That's why the story sticks. She didn't need a jeweler or a carpenter. She used what was on the floor. Catholics honor Brigid as a saint, one of Ireland's patrons alongside Patrick, and on her feast people still weave her cross with their hands.
screen: `AN OLD LIFE, FROM MEMORY.` · `HANDS ALWAYS OPEN.` · `THE ABBESS OF KILDARE.` · `A CROSS FROM THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `A CROSS FROM RUSHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make a small cross from anything. Look around where you are. Two pens. Two twigs. A pair of paper strips torn from a receipt. Two blades of grass. Lay one across the other. You don't need rushes or a pattern. Hold it in your palm. Notice how little it took. Then sit quietly with it for the time the bell gives you. If you pray, you can hold it while you pray for someone in your home, the way people do when they hang Brigid's cross by the door. If you don't, simply notice what you made from what was lying around. The bell holds the time.
Brigid of Kildare. Abbess of a great community in Ireland, honored as a saint, remembered for open hands and for the cross woven from rushes. Today's word.

Your line: a cross from rushes. Today, put the little cross you made somewhere you'll see it, a doorway, a desk, a pocket, and let it remind you that small, plain things can carry a lot. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics in Ireland and beyond keep the feast of Saint Brigid, and some families weave a Brigid's cross from rushes or straw to hang over a door or in the kitchen through the year.
